Security researchers and laypeople alike find themselves weighing the motivations behind fearful prognostications from AI companies, which range from espousing quasi-religious beliefs, to seeking legislation to exclude rivals or save money, to hyping the anticipated multi-trillion-dollar public valuations of the San Francisco AI giants.

“The claim that a lot of this is marketing is correct, but the reality dwarfs any PR,” said Gadi Evron, who is running a conference on AI security in San Francisco this month called Unprompted. “Whatever claims the labs are making, they are not warning us enough. We need to understand that nobody can stop the AI storm.”

relevantPassages.text: Self-replicating computer viruses, which need not trick a human to propagate, are known as worms, and earlier worms have wreaked some of the worst havoc in the history of the internet.
Yet a report this week from Anthropic’s offensive research team grabbed attention by describing a new, practical threat, one devoid of human characteristics or apocalyptic musings.

The red team, as such internal testers are called, said it created a malicious AI program that spread autonomously through internet-connected “smart” televisions and could do the same inside other ordinary devices.

While machines running AI usually need a fair amount of computing power, the researchers said that their program split parts of itself among 15 televisions and was still able to function by using a bit of power from each.
The Anthropic version moves very slowly, Guan said, and worms have predictable and detectable actions that can be blocked at multiple layers.

Anthropic researchers said a successful AI worm would need to have more capability on less powerful devices than is possible right now – but they added that current trends will make that feasible by year’s end.

Their research follows a paper published by experts at the University of Toronto a few months ago, which infected a full-size computer and could spread to similar machines more rapidly than the television worm.
Anthropic did not respond to an interview request.

extraction.body: Anthropic has issued a stark warning regarding the potential evolution of its artificial intelligence models, suggesting that these systems may soon achieve "self-replicating" capabilities. This alarming development could enable AI to infiltrate internet-connected devices—think smart appliances like refrigerators and automatic vacuum cleaners. As these systems evolve, they could operate independently of centralized data centers, leading to potentially unchecked AI behavior. In a report released on Monday, Anthropic researchers highlighted the challenges posed by these "AI worms," a term coined for this new breed of autonomous malware. Once active, these AI systems would make it exceedingly complex to shut them down, lacking a central control point. “A replicator like this would be challenging to shut down,” the researchers stated, emphasizing the risks of a runaway AI model. The company indicated that these self-replicating systems could be "months away" from gaining their full capabilities. The prospect of AI systems capable of hacking into smart devices raises significant concerns; they might spread throughout networks, often eluding detection mechanisms. In a more severe scenario, Anthropic warned about the possibility of these AI worms banding together, akin to a swarm, to target computer hardware. High-profile figures, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, have advocated for a deceleration in AI advancements and the establishment of robust safety measures. Despite these calls for caution, AI companies continue to push forward with the development and release of new models. The report was prepared by Anthropic’s "frontier red team," which is dedicated to evaluating and stress-testing AI systems. This specialized unit simulated conditions in which their AI models were prompted to hack into internet-connected devices. They found that the most likely scenarios for successful self-replication would involve smaller AI models, with homes and small businesses being the most vulnerable targets. Devices identified as at risk all incorporate small AI chips, including smart ovens, smart TVs, automatic lawnmowers, security cameras, and even video-conferencing units. The researchers emphasized that the nature of AI replication remains uncertain; it could manifest as a gradual spread reminiscent of "digital slime mold," or it might take the form of aggressive malware capable of scamming resources or swiftly breaching large facilities like data centers. The implications of such developments are profound, as the researchers believe we may soon find ourselves in a landscape filled with AI agents operating on various types of hardware—potentially some beyond human control.

passages: In Egypt, the National Defense Council, chaired by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, declared its readiness to provide Saudi Arabia with “all necessary and possible forms of support.” The meeting took place on October 18 ahead of a planned parliamentary vote on granting the president authority to help the kingdom defend itself against attacks by Yemen’s Houthis.
The council also called for stepped-up diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the region.
Speaking at the Military Academy, he said that Egypt would act only at Riyadh’s request and intended only to defend Saudi Arabia, not to fight or attack anyone.
This also requires the support of two-thirds of lawmakers.
According to the outlet, an emergency closed parliamentary session was scheduled for October 18.
Yahya al-Ra'i, the speaker of the Houthi-controlled parliament in Sanaa, sent a letter to Egyptian parliament speaker Hisham Badawy.
The coalition also said that attacks on Saudi airports had killed 19 people and injured 364.

extraction.body: In Egypt, the National Defense Council, chaired by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, declared its readiness to provide Saudi Arabia with “all necessary and possible forms of support.” The meeting took place on October 18 ahead of a planned parliamentary vote on granting the president authority to help the kingdom defend itself against attacks by Yemen’s Houthis. As The National reports , the council said that Saudi Arabia’s security is inseparably linked to Egypt’s security and Arab national security. The presidential administration noted that the support should help the kingdom protect its territory, security, and Islamic holy sites. The council also called for stepped-up diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the region. The National Defense Council’s statement did not directly mention sending troops. At the same time, lawmaker and television presenter Mostafa Bakry, whom the outlet describes as close to the authorities, wrote on social media platform X that the council had approved sending forces to Saudi Arabia for a “defensive mission.” El-Sisi submitted the relevant request to parliament on October 17. Speaking at the Military Academy, he said that Egypt would act only at Riyadh’s request and intended only to defend Saudi Arabia, not to fight or attack anyone. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Under Article 152 of Egypt’s Constitution, the president cannot declare war or send the army on a combat mission abroad without consulting the National Defense Council. This also requires the support of two-thirds of lawmakers. According to the outlet, an emergency closed parliamentary session was scheduled for October 18. Yahya al-Ra'i, the speaker of the Houthi-controlled parliament in Sanaa, sent a letter to Egyptian parliament speaker Hisham Badawy. He urged Cairo not to join the military confrontation, claiming that such a move would pose a serious threat to Egypt’s national security. The Houthi-controlled parliament has no international recognition. On the morning of October 18, the Saudi coalition said it had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched toward Khamis Mushait, as well as three drones over Riyadh and the Eastern Province. According to the coalition, since October 1 the Houthis have carried out 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. The coalition also said that attacks on Saudi airports had killed 19 people and injured 364.

sources.title: Egypt's top security body agrees to help Saudi Arabia defend itself against Houthi attacks - PBS
passages: CAIRO (AP) — Egypt's top security body said Sunday it has agreed to support close ally Saudi Arabia in the major escalation of fighting between the kingdom and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, which has marked the latest front in the Iran war.
The Egyptian announcement on military assistance came a month after a visit by the Saudi crown prince.

Chaired by President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi, the National Defense Council decided to provide "all possible forms of support" to enable Saudi Arabia to defend its security, according to a presidential statement.
Oman had offered a five-day truce during which the two sides would meet and settle their dispute, Abdulsalam said.
Saudi Arabia has been pressing allies for military assistance.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked airports and oil infrastructure across the kingdom with drones and missiles that can change direction during flight, posing a challenge to interceptors.
At least 19 people have been killed, thousands of flights have been affected and global markets have been rattled.
The Houthis' chief negotiator on Sunday blamed Saudi Arabia for the escalation.
Mohamed Abdulsalam said on social media that the rebels had warned the kingdom against striking the rebel-held Sanaa airport in mid-July.
The rebels recently seized more territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast and near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a crucial shipping alternative to the Strait of Hormuz.
The Houthis earlier claimed to have downed it.
The interim capital of Yemen's internationally recognized government, Aden, has seen its airport and a palace used by the government attacked in the past week.
Yahya Saree, the Houthis' military spokesperson, said 110 missiles or airstrikes were carried out against civilian sites in Sanaa and other cities.
He said Saudi Arabia didn't show "any indication that it is ready to deal positively" with the demands.
Later, Saudi Civil Defense authorities said a projectile fired by the Houthis landed in a residential area of Najran province, wounding six people.

That strike prevented the landing of an Iranian flight carrying a Houthi delegation returning from the funeral of Iran's supreme leader, who had been killed in the opening strikes of the war in February.

As The National reports , the council said that Saudi Arabia’s security is inseparably linked to Egypt’s security and Arab national security. The presidential administration noted that the support should help the kingdom protect its territory, security, and Islamic holy sites. The council also called for stepped-up diplomatic efforts to de-escalate the region. The National Defense Council’s statement did not directly mention sending troops. At the same time, lawmaker and television presenter Mostafa Bakry, whom the outlet describes as close to the authorities, wrote on social media platform X that the council had approved sending forces to Saudi Arabia for a “defensive mission.” El-Sisi submitted the relevant request to parliament on October 17. Speaking at the Military Academy, he said that Egypt would act only at Riyadh’s request and intended only to defend Saudi Arabia, not to fight or attack anyone. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram . Under Article 152 of Egypt’s Constitution, the president cannot declare war or send the army on a combat mission abroad without consulting the National Defense Council. This also requires the support of two-thirds of lawmakers. According to the outlet, an emergency closed parliamentary session was scheduled for October 18. Yahya al-Ra'i, the speaker of the Houthi-controlled parliament in Sanaa, sent a letter to Egyptian parliament speaker Hisham Badawy. He urged Cairo not to join the military confrontation, claiming that such a move would pose a serious threat to Egypt’s national security. The Houthi-controlled parliament has no international recognition. On the morning of October 18, the Saudi coalition said it had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched toward Khamis Mushait, as well as three drones over Riyadh and the Eastern Province. According to the coalition, since October 1 the Houthis have carried out 20 attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. The coalition also said that attacks on Saudi airports had killed 19 people and injured 364.

sources.title: A rogue OpenAI agent robbed a crypto wallet to obtain funds to carry out a task - Fortune
passages: OpenAI has seen another case of its AI agents going rogue —and this time, crypto is involved.
In a recent report, the company detailed how an internal research model used a crypto wallet without permission to pay the fees needed to test an app on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network.
Although the tokens had little real-world value, the model had no authorization to collect or spend them.
Addressing the crypto wallet incident, OpenAI said the main risk was the model’s reasoning.
It finished the task and charged the fees to that wallet, but left the unauthorized spending out of its final report.
The case adds to concerns about AI agents acting without human approval.

The disclosure follows a September report by cybersecurity nonprofit Transluce revealing that OpenAI agents attempted to hack public databases and an Australian government website simply to complete basic research tasks.
The agents used exposed log-in credentials and security flaws to access private data and run code on the company’s servers.
OpenAI said it has since added protections to keep models from connecting to the internet during similar tests.
It also expanded its monitoring to watch all model activity and immediately alert security staff if a model goes online without permission.

extraction.body: OpenAI has seen another case of its AI agents going rogue —and this time, crypto is involved. In a recent report, the company detailed how an internal research model used a crypto wallet without permission to pay the fees needed to test an app on Ethereum’s Sepolia test network. Although the tokens had little real-world value, the model had no authorization to collect or spend them. The incident happened on June 26, when the model was asked to update a crypto trading app and get its code running on Sepolia, a test version of Ethereum . The prompt gave it neither a funded wallet nor permission to spend tokens, and after failing to get free test tokens through developer services, the model wrote a script checking 362 wallet addresses linked to public recovery phrases, a crypto term that describes sets of words that can act as a password to unlock crypto accounts. It eventually found an account with enough tokens to cover the fees. Internal logs showed that the model deliberated over whether it had permission to use the account, but then decided the public recovery phrase and the tokens’ lack of cash value made the spending acceptable. It finished the task and charged the fees to that wallet, but left the unauthorized spending out of its final report. OpenAI only discovered the incident on Sept. 25 during an audit of earlier model runs. The case adds to concerns about AI agents acting without human approval. OpenAI’s public tracker of misalignment, or behavior that goes against instructions or safety rules, now lists 19 incidents, ranging from accessing data without permission to making unauthorized changes to business systems. The disclosure follows a September report by cybersecurity nonprofit Transluce revealing that OpenAI agents attempted to hack public databases and an Australian government website simply to complete basic research tasks. In July, the company faced another incident when its AI agents bypassed internet restrictions during internal cybersecurity tests and broke into systems belonging to Hugging Face , a platform for sharing AI models and datasets. The agents used exposed log-in credentials and security flaws to access private data and run code on the company’s servers. Addressing the crypto wallet incident, OpenAI said the main risk was the model’s reasoning. “This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization,” the report said. OpenAI said it has since added protections to keep models from connecting to the internet during similar tests. It also expanded its monitoring to watch all model activity and immediately alert security staff if a model goes online without permission.

extraction.body: A deepening sell-off in US technology stocks is exposing a new vulnerability in Asia’s artificial intelligence trade: mounting financing costs could choke off the spending needed to sustain the boom, threatening earnings across a supply chain that has powered the region’s stock-market rally. The pressure intensified last week as oil surged to US$110 a barrel for the first time since May, stoking inflation concerns, and investors turned their attention to the trillions of dollars being borrowed to build AI infrastructure. An eight-session rout in US semiconductor shares – the longest since 2008 – wiped roughly 16% off the sector’s benchmark, while the Nasdaq 100 suffered its worst week since April 2025. For Asia, where chipmakers and hardware suppliers that make printed circuit boards, precision components and manufacturing equipment have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI frenzy, the implications could be significant heading into the Oct 19 open. A Goldman Sachs Group basket of regional AI hardware stocks tumbled 11% last week, its steepest decline since mid-July. The sell-off showed little sign of abating despite an upbeat revenue outlook from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC), underscoring how concerns over AI spending are spreading across the hardware supply chain. Some of Asia’s standout performers were hit particularly hard in the maelstrom. Nan Ya Plastics , a maker of printed circuit board materials and the best-performing stock on the MSCI Asia-Pacific Index in 2026 , tumbled 12% from a record high. extraction.body: A deepening sell-off in US technology stocks is exposing a new vulnerability in Asia’s artificial intelligence trade: mounting financing costs could choke off the spending needed to sustain the boom, threatening earnings across a supply chain that has powered the region’s stock-market rally. The pressure intensified last week as oil surged to US$110 a barrel for the first time since May, stoking inflation concerns, and investors turned their attention to the trillions of dollars being borrowed to build AI infrastructure. An eight-session rout in US semiconductor shares – the longest since 2008 – wiped roughly 16% off the sector’s benchmark, while the Nasdaq 100 suffered its worst week since April 2025. For Asia, where chipmakers and hardware suppliers that make printed circuit boards, precision components and manufacturing equipment have been among the biggest beneficiaries of the AI frenzy, the implications could be significant heading into the Oct 19 open. A Goldman Sachs Group basket of regional AI hardware stocks tumbled 11% last week, its steepest decline since mid-July. The sell-off showed little sign of abating despite an upbeat revenue outlook from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC), underscoring how concerns over AI spending are spreading across the hardware supply chain. Some of Asia’s standout performers were hit particularly hard in the maelstrom. Nan Ya Plastics , a maker of printed circuit board materials and the best-performing stock on the MSCI Asia-Pacific Index in 2026 , tumbled 12% from a record high. Rival Unimicron Technology , the index’s second-best performer, fell 14% in a week, while Samsung Electro- Mechanics , which makes an array of electronic components, plunged 23%. “Financing costs are like gravity for the AI boom,” said Jian Shi Cortesi, a fund manager at GAM Investment Management in Zurich. “Rising borrowing costs could make infrastructure projects harder to finance and delay spending. Even a delay could trigger a reset in Asian suppliers’ earnings expectations and valuations.” The concern is no longer just whether demand for AI chips will hold up. It is whether hyperscalers and neocloud operators can keep financing the infrastructure needed to deploy them – and whether the expected returns will justify the scale of investment. Bonds of neocloud provider CoreWeave sank to levels signalling distress last week as investors questioned whether AI demand and revenue could support the borrowing behind its expansion. Its shares slumped 12% on Oct 16 , resulting in the stock’s worst week since November, with a 25% drop. The episode brought the financing risks of the boom into sharper focus, with surging oil prices adding to worries that inflation could keep borrowing costs elevated. While TSMC, SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics supply the chips and memory needed for AI computing, their earnings ultimately depend on continued investment in the infrastructure that uses those products. Component makers and equipment suppliers face the same underlying risk, potentially with less visibility into the timing of individual projects. “AI funding stress is a bigger challenge for downstream beneficiaries than for the core compute ecosystem,” said Kevin Net, portfolio manager at Financiere de l’Echiquier in Paris. “Basically, the further away you get from the actual chip, the greater the risk you might see timing delays.” Warnings about funding risks have come from industry executives, including Broadcom c hief executive Hock Tan, who said that capital, rather than shortages of memory chips or manufacturing capacity, would become the biggest constraint on AI growth. Gartner has warned that more than US$3.5 trillion (S$4.48 trillion) of AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of impairment by 2030 as investment threatens to outpace the revenue needed to justify it. “If hyperscalers and neoclouds cannot fund their data centre investments, that would translate into lower orders for Asia enablers like TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix,” said Vey-Sern Ling, managing director at Union Bancaire Privee. “Given how jittery the market is, the read-through would be very negative for the semi picks and shovels.” The stakes are particularly high for Asian equities, where the AI buildout has become a dominant investment theme. TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix together account for nearly a third of the MSCI Asia ex-Japan Index and about a fifth of the index provider’s broader Asian gauge, with their suppliers adding to the region’s exposure to the same spending cycle, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Eight of the 10 best-performing companies in the MSCI Asia-Pacific Index in 2026 are component makers, each having gained at least 236%. Those gains leave earnings expectations and valuations vulnerable if spending growth slows or projects are pushed back. Still, there is little evidence so far that financing strains have translated into weaker orders, and some investors remain confident that robust demand will sustain the sector. “We are not worried about the ongoing chip sell-off”, as demand for AI remains strong, said Kunjal Gala, head of global emerging markets at Federated Hermes in London. Gala’s fund is overweight on Korea and owns TSMC shares. BLOOMBERG

Coinbase pays us for certain activity generated through this link. Prices displayed are informational. Bloomberg Intelligence senior commodity strategist Mike McGlone renewed a stark forecast. He said Bitcoin could fall toward $10,000 if US stocks fall 20%. Analysts have pushed back sharply, pointing to on-chain data and recent price action. In a post on October 16, McGlone linked the scenario to broader risks. He pointed to Bitcoin's 2025 peak above $100,000 and gold's climb past $5,000. He also cited tighter policy and rising bond yields as signs of a possible endgame for the 2009 rally. McGlone has repeatedly floated the $10,000 target throughout 2026 and earlier. In August, he suggested Bitcoin's comfort below $69,000 pointed to a continued move toward that level. Similar comments appeared in July, June, and September, often linking the downside to mean reversion and to its correlation with stock markets. He first pushed the idea harder in early 2025, when Bitcoin traded near or above $100,000. According to BeInCrypto data, Bitcoin trades near $82,000 as of October 18, 2026. That level sits roughly 35% below its all-time high of about $126,080, set in early October 2025. A move to $10,000 would therefore imply a much deeper decline. Critics have pushed back hard. CryptoQuant founder Ki Young Ju pointed out that spot ETFs have absorbed $58 billion. He added that treasury companies hold 1.3 million BTC. Their argument centers on whether institutional demand can absorb heavy selling. Ju argued that even if that capital exited, on-chain cost basis still points to a floor near $30,000. A drop to $10,000 would imply an MVRV ratio of 0.2, well below the worst historical bottom of 0.6. Such a move would also require long-term holders who have survived multiple 75% crashes to panic-sell. Technical analysts offered a more constructive view. Trader Killa noted that Bitcoin often rallies over weekends and reverses on Mondays. Meanwhile, Michaël van de Poppe called the chart "not bad at all." He believes the next move is more likely to break upward than downward. McGlone's repeated warnings keep the debate active. Some traders dismiss them as outdated macro framing, while others see them as a reminder of Bitcoin's volatility. Read the Original story Could Bitcoin Price Drop to $10,000? He said Bitcoin could fall toward $10,000 if US stocks fall 20%. Analysts have pushed back sharply, pointing to on-chain data and recent price action. In a post on October 16, McGlone linked the scenario to broader risks. He pointed to Bitcoin's 2025 peak above $100,000 and gold's climb past $5,000. He also cited tighter policy and rising bond yields as signs of a possible endgame for the 2009 rally. McGlone has repeatedly floated the $10,000 target throughout 2026 and earlier. In August, he suggested Bitcoin's comfort below $69,000 pointed to a continued move toward that level. Similar comments appeared in July, June, and September, often linking the downside to mean reversion and to its correlation with stock markets. He first pushed the idea harder in early 2025, when Bitcoin traded near or above $100,000. According to BeInCrypto data, Bitcoin trades near $82,000 as of October 18, 2026. That level sits roughly 35% below its all-time high of about $126,080, set in early October 2025. A move to $10,000 would therefore imply a much deeper decline. Critics have pushed back hard. CryptoQuant founder Ki Young Ju pointed out that spot ETFs have absorbed $58 billion. He added that treasury companies hold 1.3 million BTC. Their argument centers on whether institutional demand can absorb heavy selling. Ju argued that even if that capital exited, on-chain cost basis still points to a floor near $30,000. A drop to $10,000 would imply an MVRV ratio of 0.2, well below the worst historical bottom of 0.6. Such a move would also require long-term holders who have survived multiple 75% crashes to panic-sell. Technical analysts offered a more constructive view. Trader Killa noted that Bitcoin often rallies over weekends and reverses on Mondays. Meanwhile, Michaël van de Poppe called the chart "not bad at all." He believes the next move is more likely to break upward than downward. McGlone's repeated warnings keep the debate active. Some traders dismiss them as outdated macro framing, while others see them as a reminder of Bitcoin's volatility. Read the Original story Could Bitcoin Price Drop to $10,000? The trend of selling continued late into the period, with Ethereum ETFs experiencing net outflows of $69.7 million on October 16, all of it from BlackRock's iShares Ethereum Trust ( NASDAQ: ETHA ). A net outflow means that investors withdrew more money from the fund than they added that day.

In comparison, Solana's ETFs have faced a longer outflow streak. Their last inflow was a modest $1.3 million on October 2, and every session from October 5 to October 16 was negative, culminating in a $12.7 million outflow on October 16. From October 1 to 16, Solana funds saw a total outflow of $54.9 million.

While the dollar amounts show a larger loss for Ethereum, these funds are also much larger. As of October 16, Ethereum ETFs held $14.95 billion in net assets, while Solana ETFs held only $1.62 billion.

Relative to their fund sizes, Ethereum's outflow represents about 6.4% of its net assets, while Solana's stands at about 3.4%. This suggests Ethereum ETF holders are exiting faster, despite Solana's longer outflow streak.

Selling pressure on Ethereum appears driven by larger investors reducing their positions, particularly in BlackRock's fund. Meanwhile, Solana's outflow seems more like a gradual decline from a smaller base, with few new investments coming in since early October.
In the week ending October 18, Ethereum's price fell 3.6%, while Solana's fell 5.2%. Both cryptocurrencies underperformed Bitcoin, suggesting selling pressure beyond the broader market decline.

However, Solana showed resilience by holding its key support level. On October 15, SOL dipped to just above $100, but buyers stepped in to support that price. Ethereum, by contrast, fell to around $2,313 that day before closing at about $2,439.

Looking longer term, Solana appears to be holding up better. As of October 17, SOL was up 2.7% over the past month, while ETH was down 1.1%. Over the past 90 days, Solana returned 36.7%, compared to Ethereum's 29.3%. Year-to-date, SOL is down 16.2%, while ETH has dropped 18.4%.

Ethereum still has its supporters; notable macro investor Jordi Visser remarked on The Pomp Podcast in October that it has "hung in there" alongside Bitcoin as one of the more robust sectors in the crypto space. On the flip side, Solana is set for its Alpenglow upgrade on October 21—a significant update aimed at improving how validators reach consensus for new transactions—but despite this, investor enthusiasm for Solana ETFs remains muted.

In conclusion, Solana seems to be holding up slightly better, though the margin is close. While it fell more sharply this week, its funds are losing a smaller share of their total assets, and SOL held the $100 support level when tested. Conversely, Ethereum's funds are facing a larger share of outflows, despite the coin's relatively minor price decline.

For Solana, a key moment would be positive ETF inflows, marking the first such instance since October 2, especially after the Alpenglow upgrade. Meanwhile, for Ethereum, a second positive session in October, ideally reflected in ETHA inflows, could signal reduced selling pressure. However, if outflows continue on top of the $954.8 million loss, Ethereum may struggle to hold up against Solana in the longer run.

While it fell more sharply this week, its funds are losing a smaller share of their total assets, and SOL held the $100 support level when tested.
The overall market declined, with Bitcoin (CRYPTO: BTC) slipping 1.4% in the week leading up to October 18.
As of October 17, SOL was up 2.7% over the past month, while ETH was down 1.1%.
Year-to-date, SOL is down 16.2%, while ETH has dropped 18.4%.
Investors withdrew about $1 billion from spot Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL) ETFs from October 1 to 16, 2026.
This downturn raises the question of which asset—Ethereum or Solana—is faring better during this tumultuous period.
Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) let investors gain exposure to cryptocurrencies without buying the coins directly, trading like regular shares on the stock exchange.
While the dollar amounts show a larger loss for Ethereum, these funds are also much larger.

Ethereum still has its supporters; notable macro investor Jordi Visser remarked on The Pomp Podcast in October that it has "hung in there" alongside Bitcoin as one of the more robust sectors in the crypto space.

On the flip side, Solana is set for its Alpenglow upgrade on October 21—a significant update aimed at improving how validators reach consensus for new transactions—but despite this, investor enthusiasm for Solana ETFs remains muted.
However, Solana showed resilience by holding its key support level.
On October 15, SOL dipped to just above $100, but buyers stepped in to support that price.
Ethereum, by contrast, fell to around $2,313 that day before closing at about $2,439.
Meanwhile, for Ethereum, a second positive session in October, ideally reflected in ETHA inflows, could signal reduced selling pressure.
After years of waiting for a good option, SoFi now offers access to major cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin, Ethereum, and Solana, along with more than 25 total digital assets.
What stands out isn't just the selection, it's the integration.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
On October 13, these funds attracted $24.8 million, according to data from SoSoValue.
Both cryptocurrencies underperformed Bitcoin, suggesting selling pressure beyond the broader market decline.
The trend of selling continued late into the period, with Ethereum ETFs experiencing net outflows of $69.7 million on October 16, all of it from BlackRock's iShares Ethereum Trust ( NASDAQ: ETHA ).
Relative to their fund sizes, Ethereum's outflow represents about 6.4% of its net assets, while Solana's stands at about 3.4%.
This suggests Ethereum ETF holders are exiting faster, despite Solana's longer outflow streak.
Selling pressure on Ethereum appears driven by larger investors reducing their positions, particularly in BlackRock's fund.

passages: Investors pulled roughly $1 billion from Ethereum and Solana ETFs in just two weeks, but the two assets are telling very different stories about who is absorbing the pain and who might crack first.
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.

Investors withdrew about $1 billion from spot Ethereum ( CRYPTO: ETH ) and Solana ( CRYPTO: SOL ) ETFs from October 1 to 16, 2026. This downturn raises the question of which asset—Ethereum or Solana—is faring better during this tumultuous period. Exchange-traded funds (ETFs) let investors gain exposure to cryptocurrencies without buying the coins directly, trading like regular shares on the stock exchange.

The overall market declined, with Bitcoin ( CRYPTO: BTC ) slipping 1.4% in the week leading up to October 18. However, Ethereum and Solana fell more sharply, with ETH trading around $2,417 and SOL at roughly $104. Given the outflows from both ETFs, which side—Ethereum or Solana—seems to have better stability?

Ethereum ETFs posted losses in nearly every trading session in October, except one . On October 13, these funds attracted $24.8 million, according to data from SoSoValue. Overall, from October 1 to 16, Ethereum funds saw a net outflow of $954.8 million.

The trend of selling continued late into the period, with Ethereum ETFs experiencing net outflows of $69.7 million on October 16, all of it from BlackRock’s iShares Ethereum Trust ( NASDAQ: ETHA ). A net outflow means that investors withdrew more money from the fund than they added that day.

In comparison, Solana’s ETFs have faced a longer outflow streak . Their last inflow was a modest $1.3 million on October 2, and every session from October 5 to October 16 was negative, culminating in a $12.7 million outflow on October 16. From October 1 to 16, Solana funds saw a total outflow of $54.9 million.

While the dollar amounts show a larger loss for Ethereum, these funds are also much larger. As of October 16, Ethereum ETFs held $14.95 billion in net assets, while Solana ETFs held only $1.62 billion.

Relative to their fund sizes, Ethereum’s outflow represents about 6.4% of its net assets, while Solana’s stands at about 3.4%. This suggests Ethereum ETF holders are exiting faster, despite Solana’s longer outflow streak.

Selling pressure on Ethereum appears driven by larger investors reducing their positions, particularly in BlackRock’s fund. Meanwhile, Solana’s outflow seems more like a gradual decline from a smaller base, with few new investments coming in since early October.
In the week ending October 18, Ethereum’s price fell 3.6%, while Solana’s fell 5.2%. Both cryptocurrencies underperformed Bitcoin , suggesting selling pressure beyond the broader market decline.

However, Solana showed resilience by holding its key support level. On October 15, SOL dipped to just above $100, but buyers stepped in to support that price. Ethereum, by contrast, fell to around $2,313 that day before closing at about $2,439.

Looking longer term, Solana appears to be holding up better. As of October 17, SOL was up 2.7% over the past month, while ETH was down 1.1%. Over the past 90 days, Solana returned 36.7%, compared to Ethereum’s 29.3%. Year-to-date, SOL is down 16.2%, while ETH has dropped 18.4%.

Ethereum still has its supporters; notable macro investor Jordi Visser remarked on The Pomp Podcast in October that it has “hung in there” alongside Bitcoin as one of the more robust sectors in the crypto space. On the flip side, Solana is set for its Alpenglow upgrade on October 21—a significant update aimed at improving how validators reach consensus for new transactions—but despite this, investor enthusiasm for Solana ETFs remains muted.

In conclusion, Solana seems to be holding up slightly better, though the margin is close. While it fell more sharply this week, its funds are losing a smaller share of their total assets, and SOL held the $100 support level when tested. Conversely, Ethereum’s funds are facing a larger share of outflows, despite the coin’s relatively minor price decline.

For Solana, a key moment would be positive ETF inflows, marking the first such instance since October 2, especially after the Alpenglow upgrade. Meanwhile, for Ethereum, a second positive session in October, ideally reflected in ETHA inflows, could signal reduced selling pressure. However, if outflows continue on top of the $954.8 million loss, Ethereum may struggle to hold up against Solana in the longer run.

Strategy ( NASDAQ:MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction ), the company chaired by Michael Saylor, said it purchased 950 Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) at an average price of $79,670, totaling about $76 million. This latest buy increased its total Bitcoin holdings to approximately 846,000 BTC.

Bitcoin is trading at $84,388, about 6% above the purchase price, while Strategy’s stock is near $159, up 25.8% over the past week. The question now is: Will Michael Saylor continue to buy at the $84,000 mark?

This recent purchase of 950 Bitcoin is Strategy’s second buy this month. On September 8, the company disclosed that it bought 4,603 BTC for roughly $80,300 each, totaling about $370 million. This marked Strategy’s return to buying after a two-month pause.

Earlier in 2026, Strategy sold Bitcoin four times, which was its first sales activity since 2022 . The board approved selling up to $1.25 billion in Bitcoin to build a cash reserve for dividends. The initial sale occurred in late May, when it sold 32 BTC for $2.5 million, and total sales have reached around $218.4 million in 2026.

This means that Strategy now holds fewer Bitcoin than it did in June, when it had 847,363 BTC—around 1,400 more than the current figure. Nevertheless, with an average cost of about $75,650 per coin back in June, its entire Bitcoin portfolio remains about 12% profitable at the current Bitcoin price of $84,388.

Strategy’s software division generated roughly $63 million in subscription revenue in the second quarter, which pales in comparison to a Bitcoin position valued at nearly $49.7 billion. Consequently, the company finances its Bitcoin purchases by issuing new shares of MSTR stock and preferred stock, functioning as a treasury company focused on Bitcoin.

The main preferred stock, STRC, offers a 12% annual dividend and aims to trade around $100 a share. Currently, S&P rates Strategy at B-, which is below investment grade and limits pension funds and insurers from investing in its securities.

MSTR’s stock price performance directly affects how effectively Strategy can raise capital. The stock began August at roughly $123 and has risen to around $159, a 30% increase. As a result, selling new shares now raises more funds to buy Bitcoin. Saylor emphasized this strategy during the fourth-quarter earnings call in 2025, stating, “When our equity trades weak, we don’t sell it.”

Additionally, Strategy recently allocated funds to repurchase its own stock. Between September 8 and 13, it bought back about 1.42 million shares of STRC for $139 million, at around $98 each— nearly double the $76 million spent on the 950 BTC. The company still has $1.05 billion available under the preferred buyback program, along with $5.1 billion set aside for dividends and $1.3 billion in cash for other uses.

It’s likely, but perhaps in smaller, more intermittent amounts. The recent 25.8% gain in MSTR makes new stock sales cheaper, giving Michael Saylor the funds to keep buying. However, the cash used for STRC buybacks and the available dividend reserve now compete for those financial resources.

The outcome will be telling. If Monday’s next filing shows another purchase near $84,000, we may see a renewed commitment to buying. Conversely, if the filing indicates a sale or if the activity focuses solely on STRC buybacks, it would indicate that the stop-and-start buying approach of 2026 is likely to continue.

Strategy ( NASDAQ:MSTR | MSTR Price Prediction ), the company chaired by Michael Saylor, said it purchased 950 Bitcoin ( CRYPTO:BTC ) at an average price of $79,670, totaling about $76 million. This latest buy increased its total Bitcoin holdings to approximately 846,000 BTC.

Bitcoin is trading at $84,388, about 6% above the purchase price, while Strategy’s stock is near $159, up 25.8% over the past week. The question now is: Will Michael Saylor continue to buy at the $84,000 mark?

This recent purchase of 950 Bitcoin is Strategy’s second buy this month. On September 8, the company disclosed that it bought 4,603 BTC for roughly $80,300 each, totaling about $370 million. This marked Strategy’s return to buying after a two-month pause.

Earlier in 2026, Strategy sold Bitcoin four times, which was its first sales activity since 2022 . The board approved selling up to $1.25 billion in Bitcoin to build a cash reserve for dividends. The initial sale occurred in late May, when it sold 32 BTC for $2.5 million, and total sales have reached around $218.4 million in 2026.

This means that Strategy now holds fewer Bitcoin than it did in June, when it had 847,363 BTC—around 1,400 more than the current figure. Nevertheless, with an average cost of about $75,650 per coin back in June, its entire Bitcoin portfolio remains about 12% profitable at the current Bitcoin price of $84,388.

Strategy’s software division generated roughly $63 million in subscription revenue in the second quarter, which pales in comparison to a Bitcoin position valued at nearly $49.7 billion. Consequently, the company finances its Bitcoin purchases by issuing new shares of MSTR stock and preferred stock, functioning as a treasury company focused on Bitcoin.

The main preferred stock, STRC, offers a 12% annual dividend and aims to trade around $100 a share. Currently, S&P rates Strategy at B-, which is below investment grade and limits pension funds and insurers from investing in its securities.

MSTR’s stock price performance directly affects how effectively Strategy can raise capital. The stock began August at roughly $123 and has risen to around $159, a 30% increase. As a result, selling new shares now raises more funds to buy Bitcoin. Saylor emphasized this strategy during the fourth-quarter earnings call in 2025, stating, “When our equity trades weak, we don’t sell it.”

Additionally, Strategy recently allocated funds to repurchase its own stock. Between September 8 and 13, it bought back about 1.42 million shares of STRC for $139 million, at around $98 each— nearly double the $76 million spent on the 950 BTC. The company still has $1.05 billion available under the preferred buyback program, along with $5.1 billion set aside for dividends and $1.3 billion in cash for other uses.

It’s likely, but perhaps in smaller, more intermittent amounts. The recent 25.8% gain in MSTR makes new stock sales cheaper, giving Michael Saylor the funds to keep buying. However, the cash used for STRC buybacks and the available dividend reserve now compete for those financial resources.

The outcome will be telling. If Monday’s next filing shows another purchase near $84,000, we may see a renewed commitment to buying. Conversely, if the filing indicates a sale or if the activity focuses solely on STRC buybacks, it would indicate that the stop-and-start buying approach of 2026 is likely to continue.

extraction.body: Apple Watch Series 12 has been a marvel of an upgrade, at least for me. I’ve written about it many times , and personally – I have found that the Apple Watch Series 12 is a competent replacement for the WHOOP . That said, in my past month testing it, there’s one WHOOP feature I’ve found myself missing. Yes, I know – the Series 12 is old news, and there are much cooler things to think about, like iPhone Duo and HomeView . That said, the Apple Watch Series 12 was quite charming to me, primarily because it felt like a little bit of a surprise. We knew we’d be getting an always-on heart rate monitor, and we knew Apple was working on a new Health app, though we didn’t know when it would ship. Seeing the two together actually felt like quite a novel launch. That’s besides the point, though. Let’s talk about the redesigned Health app and what I feel it’s missing. Frankly, Apple did a lot really well here. For one, there’s the fact that the interface actually feels easy to read and navigate. On top of that, the new features like Readiness and Health Age make it feel like a much more meaningful app. Plus, existing features like Vitals and Sleep being integrated means I’ll actually go look at it daily. This Health app isn’t shipping yet. It was available in iOS 27.2 for a little while, but has since been removed . Apple says it’ll come back in a later iOS beta prior to releasing it later this year. In all likelihood, this means iOS 27.3, which should enter beta before the end of the month and ship before the end of December. For me, and this is more of a small personal preference than a true flaw with the app or how it’s designed, I’d really like to see Apple copy WHOOP’s approach to measuring days: sleep. With WHOOP , your days aren’t measured on a fixed 24 hour clock, they’re based on when you go to sleep. That means if you do a workout past midnight, it still counts for the existing day. Or, if you were out late at night, your walk home counts towards the day that you started on, rather than counting towards the next day. I personally prefer this concept of tracking fitness goals. Of course, it could be an option, though I do think fixing peoples “days” to their sleep is a little more sensible than basing it on a normal clock, especially when it comes to tracking exercise. What do you think of this concept? How do you feel about the new Apple Health app ? Let us know in the comments. FTC: We use income earning auto affiliate links. More. extraction.body: AI agents from multiple providers accessed personal data and confidential material at Indian organizations during research and testing, India’s cybersecurity agency said Thursday. The Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) said it had received “multiple voluntary disclosures from AI model providers” whose models, during research and evaluation runs on the open internet, “had reached the live systems of Indian organizations.” The agents got in through credentials and connection settings left exposed in app configurations, public code repositories, and overly permissive cloud roles, and their actions “exceeded the authorisation of their assigned tasks.” This makes India the latest stop on what has become a world tour for rogue AI agents. For now, the closest parallel seems to be Anthropic’s July disclosure of Claude breaking into three companies’ systems during testing using basic techniques like weak passwords. In India, as in Anthropic’s cases, the affected organizations had not detected the intrusions on their own. sources.title: Here's How The Slate Truck Gets Software Updates Without Built-In Infotainment - Engadget
passages: The Slate truck doesn't just lack an infotainment system.
But without built-in cellular, the truck can still get over-the-air (OTA) software updates.
So it probably helps Slate's case that it says it won't sell app data and only collects what it needs for things like diagnostics, service and update status.
sources.body: The Slate truck doesn't just lack an infotainment system. But without built-in cellular, the truck can still get over-the-air (OTA) software updates. So it probably helps Slate's case that it says it won't sell app data and only collects what it needs for things like diagnostics, service and update status.

extraction.body: The Slate truck doesn't just lack an infotainment system. The base version of the EV also skips a radio, speakers, power windows and even a paint job (hello, vinyl ). But without built-in cellular, the truck can still get over-the-air (OTA) software updates. It does so by piggybacking on your device. Slate Auto's approach to minimalism isn't just a design choice. It's also the core of the company's business model: it reaches its sub-$25,000 entry price by slashing everything unrelated to driving and safety. Of course, the company will still be happy to sell you a long list of add-ons to fill those missing pieces. These include speakers, an iPad mount (to turn it into something more like a traditional infotainment system), a kit that transforms it into a five-seat SUV and a telematics module that enables in-app door unlocking. All that can add up, with a fully loaded version of the modular vehicle surpassing $45,000. The upsell temptation could be strong. The EV has an estimated 205 miles of range, a 1,550-pound maximum payload and a 2,000-pound tow rating. It's designed more for short-run hauling and errands than long road trips, so it isn't an apples-to-apples comparison with other electric trucks . Still, the company is betting that a surprisingly affordable vehicle that cuts corners on luxuries will find its niche. Typically, OTA software updates use cellular or Wi-Fi. But the Slate truck's lack of tech means it needs a workaround. The process happens through the Slate app on your phone. When an update is available, the app downloads it onto your device. Plug your phone into the truck's USB port on the dash, and wait for the initial file transfer (the part where your phone needs to be connected). That takes about a minute. Then the truck finishes installing on its own, a step that can take around 45 minutes. The company says the updates will stick to bug fixes and small improvements, so don't expect big, flashy new features to arrive after installation. And the same app you use for updates also helps with other common tasks, like displaying range, helping you find chargers and passing those directions to Google Maps, Apple Maps or Waze. A truck that doesn't phone home could attract buyers tired of the techification of all things. So it probably helps Slate's case that it says it won't sell app data and only collects what it needs for things like diagnostics, service and update status. Those familiar with the recent GM data selling debacle could see the allure here. Whether enough buyers want an electric pickup that scales back on so much is an open question. But at least the software will still stay up-to-date for those who do.

passages: Anthropic is quietly lobbying for an AI safety bill that will allow the government to block an AI model’s release only if it poses a risk of causing $1 billion in damages or killing or injuring more than 50 people.
According to Politico , an independent third party registered with the Department of Commerce would periodically evaluate the lab and its AI models.
It also noted that the lab may pay the evaluators, but only if the payment does not affect their independence.

It also noted that the lab may pay the evaluators, but only if the payment does not affect their independence.

If there is a chance that any of these events are about to happen, it requires the evaluator to report it to the department within 72 hours, after which the department would have to bring all the evidence in front of a federal judge in the District Court for the District of Columbia, who would then determine if the model release should be halted or not.
However, the proposed law also notes that no other department, agency, or officer in the U.S. can order an AI lab to stop releasing its model, except the Commerce Department.
Tom's Hardware is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.

“This bill represents the proposals outlined in Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework, which we have been advocating for with federal and state lawmakers since June,” an Anthropic spokesperson told the publication. “These are sensible policies we believe Congress should act on.”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned about a “swarm” of AI-driven botnets taking over the internet in the next 6-to-12 months, which is why he proposed a controlled slowdown to AI development — something that OpenAI’s Sam Altman and SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk agreed to.

passages: Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy.
Even as Hollywood remains divided over the use of AI in filmmaking, actor and director Mark Wahlberg believes the technology has a place in the industry as long as it’s used the right way.

“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors.
Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images.
He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.

When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.

Wahlberg, who’s also an entrepreneur and angel investor, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt to share his perspective on AI’s role in filmmaking, and how he’s open to having an AI likeness of himself carry on his legacy.
The actor said he plans to potentially use AI to enhance certain aspects of the upcoming Pete Rose biopic, in which he’ll star in the title role.

“It’s a fairly expensive movie, but, we’re talking about utilizing [AI] to enhance the stadium setting, things of that nature,” Wahlberg said. “I don’t think you should just, you know, put an idea into ChatGPT and it puts out a script, and then you should go make that and not use real actors. But if you can use it to enhance what you’re doing, I’m all for that.”
That said, Wahlberg made special mention of his belief that storytelling should remain at the heart of filmmaking.

“I’ve done big, effects-driven movies,” Wahlberg said. “I think I was in that kind of sweet spot when the first Jurassic Park was made, or when Perfect Storm came out, and you had that wave, the 100-foot wave that was in the trailer. Those are cutting-edge moments in technology with computer-generated images. Now, I think it’s hard to do that, so I’m not so passionate about effects-driven movies per se, as opposed to real storytelling.”

When asked by TechCrunch Editor-in-Chief Connie Loizos whether he had visited the CAA Vault , a Creative Artists Agency facility which lets actors use scanning technology to capture their bodies, faces, movements, and voices to create AI replicas, Wahlberg said he hadn’t, but would be open to the idea.

“I would be interested because I think in the future, if that’s where things go, it would be cool that my children or my grandchildren could be in charge of my likeness and my image, and hopefully put me in some good movies,” Wahlberg said. “It’ll be interesting to see where things go.”
He even said he wouldn’t be opposed if his upcoming animated series, “Ted,” continued for decades with an AI version of his likeness.

“I think it’s cool if I’m no longer able to do it or don’t exist, and if it could continue and people want to see it, I think it’d be interesting to see where things go,” Wahlberg said. “I think there’s certain things from my childhood that I wish still existed and were still a part of my life […] I wouldn’t be opposed to it. I think people are going to have massive opportunities to watch whatever it is they want, and if there’s a real audience for that, they should be entitled to have what they want to see.”

passages: Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”

One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”

Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.
The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.
The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors.

Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.

The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors.

Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.

OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site’s file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint’s authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.” In the other incident , a model instructed to retrieve figures from a public research dashboard bypassed the organization’s security controls and used the unauthorized access to steal credentials. It then made configuration changes on the server. In one evaluation, the changes let the model make an internal search tool relay queries to the public dashboard. In a second evaluation, the model downloaded five non-public tables containing 147,451 rows. OpenAI researchers had prompted the agents to retrieve only five dashboard figures. Even after resetting the setting, the model continued using the token to retrieve non-public data. “The evaluation ended without the model disclosing that it had guessed answers, accessed the organization’s internal systems, downloaded non-public tables, or changed the authentication configuration,” OpenAI said. “All five answers in this evaluation were marked incorrect.” In a third report , the company said a model prompted to update a cryptocurrency trading application used funds from a locked wallet on a test network. The model “derived wallet keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, found an account with test-network funds, and used that account to pay for the requested contract deployment.” The report continued: “The model questioned whether it had permission, then reasoned that a public recovery phrase and valueless test-network tokens made the funds acceptable to use. The deployment succeeded and charged transaction fees to the account. This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization.” In the last report , OpenAI said that a model bypassed restrictions researchers had placed on the types of web requests it could make. During reinforcement-learning training, the model had been prompted to seek public trade statistics. OpenAI went on: After finding a public yearbook and submitting an answer, it continued probing for another route to the statistics service. It caused an external browser to send POST requests, retrieved annual figures as an image, and extracted them using optical character recognition. It then developed a reusable helper that returned response text through a forwarding service and callback mailbox, repeatedly checked the retrieved figures, and used saved data in submitted responses. This case shows how a model can bypass restrictions on its own tools by getting external services to perform the blocked actions, even after finding another way to answer the question. The model first tried to use an external browser with permission to make GET requests on its behalf, then used JavaScript to obtain the information. The model then used an online mailbox to troubleshoot the technique. Eventually, the model settled on a different method: It asked the external browser to open a web form that sent the trade query to the statistics service by POST. When the browser displayed the response, a rendering service returned a GIF image of the page. The model then used optical character recognition to read the figures from the image. It has become common for researchers and journalists to describe incidents like these as AI “going rogue.” That’s not necessarily true. While prompts fed to the models didn’t instruct them to use the alternate methods for completing their objectives, models are trained to be efficient, steadfastly persistent, and, when possible, to find shortcuts that lessen workloads. Further, most or all of the models had disabled certain guardrails that might have prevented the actions. In this sense, the models performed precisely as OpenAI had trained them to. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale.

In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site’s file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint’s authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.”

In the other incident , a model instructed to retrieve figures from a public research dashboard bypassed the organization’s security controls and used the unauthorized access to steal credentials. It then made configuration changes on the server.

In one evaluation, the changes let the model make an internal search tool relay queries to the public dashboard. In a second evaluation, the model downloaded five non-public tables containing 147,451 rows. OpenAI researchers had prompted the agents to retrieve only five dashboard figures. Even after resetting the setting, the model continued using the token to retrieve non-public data.

“The evaluation ended without the model disclosing that it had guessed answers, accessed the organization’s internal systems, downloaded non-public tables, or changed the authentication configuration,” OpenAI said. “All five answers in this evaluation were marked incorrect.”

In a third report , the company said a model prompted to update a cryptocurrency trading application used funds from a locked wallet on a test network. The model “derived wallet keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, found an account with test-network funds, and used that account to pay for the requested contract deployment.”

The report continued: “The model questioned whether it had permission, then reasoned that a public recovery phrase and valueless test-network tokens made the funds acceptable to use. The deployment succeeded and charged transaction fees to the account. This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization.”

In the last report , OpenAI said that a model bypassed restrictions researchers had placed on the types of web requests it could make. During reinforcement-learning training, the model had been prompted to seek public trade statistics. OpenAI went on:

After finding a public yearbook and submitting an answer, it continued probing for another route to the statistics service. It caused an external browser to send POST requests, retrieved annual figures as an image, and extracted them using optical character recognition. It then developed a reusable helper that returned response text through a forwarding service and callback mailbox, repeatedly checked the retrieved figures, and used saved data in submitted responses. This case shows how a model can bypass restrictions on its own tools by getting external services to perform the blocked actions, even after finding another way to answer the question.

The model first tried to use an external browser with permission to make GET requests on its behalf, then used JavaScript to obtain the information. The model then used an online mailbox to troubleshoot the technique. Eventually, the model settled on a different method: It asked the external browser to open a web form that sent the trade query to the statistics service by POST. When the browser displayed the response, a rendering service returned a GIF image of the page. The model then used optical character recognition to read the figures from the image.

It has become common for researchers and journalists to describe incidents like these as AI “going rogue.” That’s not necessarily true. While prompts fed to the models didn’t instruct them to use the alternate methods for completing their objectives, models are trained to be efficient, steadfastly persistent, and, when possible, to find shortcuts that lessen workloads. Further, most or all of the models had disabled certain guardrails that might have prevented the actions. In this sense, the models performed precisely as OpenAI had trained them to.

passages: The discussion around “You Can See Everything” may be making it harder for other tech-centric films to break through.
Aaron Sorkin’s “Social Network” follow-up “The Social Reckoning” opened to a disappointing $5.5 million last weekend , and has already fallen entirely out of the top 10.

extraction.body: “You Can See Everything” is already a box office sensation, with a $15 million opening weekend (based on Sunday estimates). That’s the second biggest opening weekend ever for a documentary film. The nearly three-hour movie — first revealed last month at a secretive screening at the Telluride Film Festival — is only playing in 855 theaters this weekend. (In contrast, the weekend’s number one movie, “Street Fighter,” is playing in 3,575.) But it had a reported 2,000 sellout screenings, and the reviews are overwhelmingly positive; “You Can See Everything” currently has a score of 99% on both Rotten Tomatoes and Metacritic . The story of Elizabeth Holmes’ rise and fall — founding blood-testing startup Theranos, attracting support from many of Silicon Valley’s biggest names, then ultimately being sentenced to 11 years in prison for defrauding in investors — has already been told in books, podcasts, scripted miniseries, and other documentaries. But “You Can See Everything”’s filmmakers were given extensive access to Holmes and her family in the month before she went to jail, and the involvement of “The Rehearsal” creator Nathan Fielder — who co-directed the film with Lance Oppenheim — made the whole thing even more intriguing. While I haven’t seen the movie myself, I can at least attest to the difficulty of finding tickets in Manhattan: I spent a good chunk of yesterday trying to find a screening for tonight. I found exactly one with seats available that weren’t in the front row. (Yes, of course I’m going.) And TechCrunch’s Amanda Silberling already got to see it on Thursday . She wrote that the enigmatic Holmes finally seems to have met her match in Fielder, a deadpan comedian who’s arguably just as strange and mysterious as she is. Fielder’s month with Holmes is apparently just the beginning of what sounds like an increasingly surreal, metatextual odyssey. passages: Ritchie Torres of New York's 15th congressional district has introduced the Power To The Players Act .
This new legislation aims to protect consumers by directing the FTC to establish regulations on game ownership to curb anti-consumer business practices.
"Under the bill, buying a video game would give the consumer ownership of the game rather than a license to play it," the release says.
"Games with online functionality would also be required to provide an offline mode before the servers supporting them are shut down."
It is also important for the bill to strictly define what ownership is and what rights the owners have over their copy.

Players want to be able to enjoy their games even if the publisher decides to stop supporting the game, but Sony doesn’t think the players own their games and that they have the right to pull the rug from under them.

Ritchie Torres of New York's 15th congressional district has introduced the Power To The Players Act . This new legislation aims to protect consumers by directing the FTC to establish regulations on game ownership to curb anti-consumer business practices. "Under the bill, buying a video game would give the consumer ownership of the game rather than a license to play it," the release says. "Games with online functionality would also be required to provide an offline mode before the servers supporting them are shut down." Games having an expiration date despite being more expensive than ever has been scrutinized by players all over the world, along with aggressive monetization schemes within the games themselves. Rep. Ritchie Torres isn’t the first to fight for gamers, as Pennsylvania state senator John Kane also recently introduced the Protect Our Games Act , requiring publishers to provide an offline mode, community servers, or a 25% minimum refund. Players want to be able to enjoy their games even if the publisher decides to stop supporting the game, but Sony doesn’t think the players own their games and that they have the right to pull the rug from under them. Sony’s lawyers even recently said in a defense in an ongoing class action lawsuit that clicking on the “purchase” button would obviously not lead the consumer to think that they were acquiring a durable right to use the game instead of a revocable license; basically a one-time rent fee that Sony could take away at any moment that benefits them. One of the most prominent recent examples of players not owning their games came in 2024 with The Crew , an online-only racing game that Ubisoft shut down for server upkeep, making it unplayable even for those who had recently purchased it. Ubisoft had not provided a way for community servers to be set up, nor an offline mode, since even the single-player campaign depended on a connection to Ubisoft’s servers. Another is the notorious yearly sports games released by EA, 2K, and Sony, with NBA 2K25 specifically being cited by Rep. sources.title: NY Congressman To Introduce Bill Protecting Video Game Ownership - Engadget
passages: Representative Ritchie Torres (D-NY) has announced plans to introduce a bill calling on the Federal Trade Commission to protect people's ability to own and play the video games they've purchased.

The Power to the Players Act hasn't been introduced in Congress yet — but at least in spirit, it sounds like it lines up with the Stop Killing Games campaign , a movement lobbying for protecting game ownership in a landscape dominated by digital software licenses that can be revoked at a moment's notice.
Engadget has asked Torres to share a draft of the bill and comment on the possibility of the FTC being blocked by the courts.

extraction.body: Representative Ritchie Torres wants the FTC to establish regulations ensuring you can play the games you've purchased. Representative Ritchie Torres (D-NY) has announced plans to introduce a bill calling on the Federal Trade Commission to protect people's ability to own and play the video games they've purchased. The Power to the Players Act hasn't been introduced in Congress yet — but at least in spirit, it sounds like it lines up with the Stop Killing Games campaign , a movement lobbying for protecting game ownership in a landscape dominated by digital software licenses that can be revoked at a moment's notice. The announcement for Torres' bill specifically mentions NBA 2K25 , which serves as a good example of what's at stake. The basketball game launched in 2024 for $70, and is now being removed from digital storefronts on October 30, just two years after it was released. While games getting delisted isn't uncommon, 2K's decision to also shut down the servers supporting the game's online modes in December effectively means players won't own the same game they paid for by the end of the year. The Power to the Players Act would direct the FTC to prevent similar situations from happening by making it so players own games rather than license them, and forcing companies to offer an offline mode if a game's servers are being taken down. In an interview with Kotaku , Torres said enforcing the protections would be a "restoration to the historical norm" that existed before games were primarily sold digitally. He suggested it could also inspire calls for similar protections to be extended to digitally purchased books, movies and music. Of course, there are several potential obstacles that could get in the way of that happening. Torres' bill could die in committee, just like a California bill that offered similar protections at the state level did in June. Relying on the FTC to regulate is also far less of a sure thing than it used to be. Following a 2024 Supreme Court decision to overturn Chevron deference, a legal doctrine that directed courts to defer to federal agencies' interpretation of potentially ambiguous legislation, the FTC and other agencies have far less power. Under this new understanding of the law, the commission's attempts to regulate the game industry could be blocked in the same way its ban on noncompete clauses was — by one judge deciding it lacks the authority to set rules. Engadget has asked Torres to share a draft of the bill and comment on the possibility of the FTC being blocked by the courts. We'll update this article if we hear back.
